intro: Until the Spanish Civil War, the village of Ondategi in Álava held its August festival under one oak, with one accordion for music. The Sarragoa oak, Ondategiko Haritza in Basque, is a pedunculate oak twenty metres tall with a crown about thirty metres across, standing on the communal meadow at the edge of the village. The Basque Government declared it a Singular Tree in 1997, one of ten in Álava. The festival did not survive the war; the oak did. Free, on the open meadow.
meta_description: Ondategiko Haritza, the Sarragoa oak: a pedunculate oak with a 30-metre crown where Ondategi held its festival. Free, on a communal meadow.
question_meta: Ondategiko Haritza is a protected pedunculate oak on the Sarragoa meadow in Ondategi, Álava, with a 30-metre crown. Its story and how to find it.
question_answer: Ondategiko Haritza, also called the Roble de Sarragoa, is a pedunculate oak on the campa of Sarragoa, the communal meadow at the southwest edge of Ondategi in the municipality of Zigoitia, Álava. It is about twenty metres tall with a crown around thirty metres wide and a trunk 4.9 metres round, and the Basque Government declared it a Singular Tree in 1997. It is free to visit on the open meadow.
question_context: The tree's best story is about a party. Ondategi's romería of San Lorenzo fell on 10 August, but the village could only afford paid musicians for one feast a year, Santa Lucía on 13 December. So in August the celebration took place in the shade of the Sarragoa oak with a single accordionist, and it went on that way until the Spanish Civil War, after which the romería under the tree was not revived. For generations the oak also gave shade and shelter to livestock and people on the meadow. It goes by several names: Ondategiko Haritza, Sarragoako haritza, the Roble de Sarragoa, and the plainest of them, the Árbol gordo de Zanagua, the fat tree. The Basque Government listed it as a Singular Tree in 1997, one of ten in the province of Álava, and the published measurement puts its trunk at 4.9 metres round at chest height. Every source calls it centenario, which means old and says nothing more precise. No one has published an age, and a reader who knows when the romería under it began would already be telling us more than any source does.

faq.a: No source gives an age. Every account calls it centenario, simply meaning very old. If you know more, tell us.

Until the Spanish Civil War, Ondategi held its August romería of San Lorenzo under its crown, with a single accordionist playing, because the village could afford paid musicians only for its December feast.
Yes. It stands on an open communal meadow at the edge of the village, with no gate or ticket.

Go to Ondategi, in the municipality of Zigoitia, Álava, and take the street to the left of the church to its end; the oak stands on the Sarragoa meadow. The village is about 13 kilometres from Vitoria-Gasteiz, and a car is the realistic way to get there.

trees.story:
Until the Spanish Civil War, the village of Ondategi held its summer festival under this oak, and the music was one accordion. The San Lorenzo romería fell on 10 August, and the village could afford paid musicians for only one feast a year, Santa Lucía on 13 December. So in August a single accordionist played in the shade of the Sarragoa oak, and that was the party.

The tree has the room for it. It is a pedunculate oak 20 metres tall with a crown about 30 metres across, standing on the campa of Sarragoa, the communal meadow at the southwest edge of the village, at the end of the street that runs to the left of the church. For generations it gave shade and shelter to livestock and people alike. The Basque Government declared it a Singular Tree in 1997, one of ten in Álava, and the published measurement puts the trunk at 4.9 metres round at chest height.

Locally it goes by several names: Ondategiko Haritza, Sarragoako haritza, the Roble de Sarragoa, and the plainer Árbol gordo de Zanagua, the fat tree. Every source calls it centenario, which means old and nothing more precise. Nobody has published an age, and a trunk of that size does not settle it on its own. If you know when the romería under it began, that would be a start.

The romería under its crown did not survive the war. The oak did.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its spread: an oak with a crown about 30 metres wide and a trunk 4.9 metres round, on the open meadow at the end of the street left of Ondategi's church.
